questions.stem: A 58 year old woman has noticed a painless lump in her left breast for 6 weeks. There is a 2 cm hard, irregular mass in the upper outer quadrant that is fixed to the underlying tissue. There is a firm 1 cm node in the left axilla. There is no nipple discharge. She has no fever.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A hard, irregular, painless mass fixed to deep tissue with axillary lymphadenopathy is breast cancer; invasive ductal carcinoma is the most common type.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: firm 1 cm node in the left axilla
steps.x: Hard, irregular, fixed, painless with an axillary node.

elim: Cysts are smooth, mobile and often tender, not hard and fixed with a node.
Duct ectasia causes periareolar thickening and discharge, usually around the nipple.
Fat necrosis follows trauma and does not usually cause a hard axillary node.
Fibroadenomas are smooth, mobile and occur in younger women.

steps.x: E. Invasive ductal carcinoma. Hard, irregular, fixed lump + node = invasive ductal carcinoma until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: A 53 year old woman has core biopsy after her screening mammogram. Histology shows malignant cells confined within the breast ducts with an intact basement membrane. She has no breast lump, skin changes or nipple discharge, and her examination is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on her mammogram?
o: Skin thickening over the whole breast
questions.e: DCIS (cancer confined within ducts, basement membrane intact) typically appears as microcalcification on screening mammography.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding on her mammogram? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: confined within the breast ducts with an intact basement membrane
steps.x: Histology is DCIS; what does DCIS look like on a mammogram?

elim: A smooth well-defined mass suggests a cyst or fibroadenoma.
She was recalled from screening, so the mammogram was abnormal.
This suggests inflammatory cancer or lymphatic obstruction.
This suggests invasive carcinoma.

steps.x: A. Clustered microcalcification. DCIS = microcalcification on mammography.

questions.stem: A 46 year old woman has a bilateral breast reduction for back pain. She had no lumps before surgery and a normal mammogram a year ago. Histology of the removed tissue shows small uniform cells filling and expanding the lobules, with the basement membrane intact and no invasion.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: LCIS is often an incidental finding on biopsy or surgical specimens, with cells confined to the lobules and an intact basement membrane.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Incidental lobular cells, in situ, no lump.

elim: DCIS involves ducts and usually shows microcalcification on mammography.
Fibroadenomas form a palpable mobile lump.
There is no invasion through the basement membrane.
A benign proliferation, not cells filling lobules.

steps.x: D. Lobular carcinoma in situ. LCIS is usually incidental.

questions.stem: A 59 year old woman has an area of firmness in her right breast. Her mammogram is reported as subtle architectural distortion only. Core biopsy shows small, round, uniform cells infiltrating in single-file lines through the stroma beyond the basement membrane.
questions.q: Which is the most likely histological diagnosis?
questions.e: Invasive lobular carcinoma has small round uniform cells infiltrating in single file and is hard to see on mammography.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely histological diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: small, round, uniform cells infiltrating in single-file
steps.x: Poorly seen on mammogram and small uniform infiltrating cells.

elim: In situ disease does not infiltrate beyond the basement membrane.
IDC is commonest but forms a hard discrete mass well seen on mammography.
LCIS is confined by the basement membrane.
A fibroepithelial tumour that grows rapidly to a large mass.

steps.x: C. Invasive lobular carcinoma. ILC: small uniform cells, single file, hard to see on mammogram.

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman notices that her right nipple has become pulled in over the past 3 months. It was previously normal. There is a 2 cm hard mass directly behind the nipple. There is no discharge and no pain. Her left breast is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: New unilateral nipple retraction with a hard mass behind the nipple is breast cancer until proven otherwise.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: pulled in over the past 3 months
2 cm hard mass directly behind the nipple
steps.x: Recent, unilateral nipple retraction with a hard mass.

elim: No pain, fever or redness.
Duct ectasia causes slit-like retraction with discharge, often bilateral, without a hard mass.
There is no history of trauma.
Paget's causes eczema-like skin change of the nipple, not just retraction.

steps.x: B. Breast cancer. New nipple retraction plus a hard mass = cancer.

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman has invasive ductal carcinoma of the left breast. On imaging the tumour measures 6.5 cm and does not involve the skin or chest wall. Sentinel node biopsy is negative and staging CT shows no distant spread.
questions.q: Which is the T stage of her tumour?
questions.e: T stage is by size: T1 under 2 cm, T2 2 to 5 cm, T3 over 5 cm, T4 chest wall or skin involvement.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the T stage of her tumour? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: does not involve the skin or chest wall
steps.x: Over 5 cm and no skin or chest wall involvement.

elim: T1 is under 2 cm.
T2 is 2 to 5 cm.
T4 needs chest wall or skin involvement or inflammatory disease.
Tis is in situ disease.

steps.x: C. T3. Over 5 cm = T3.

questions.stem: A 55 year old woman has a 3 cm invasive ductal carcinoma of the right breast with no skin involvement. Axillary node clearance finds metastatic carcinoma in 5 of 18 axillary lymph nodes. Staging CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis shows no distant spread.
questions.q: Which is the most likely TNM stage?
questions.e: T2 is 2 to 5 cm; N2 is 4 to 9 local nodes; M0 is no distant metastasis.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely TNM stage? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Size 3 cm, 5 nodes, no metastasis.

elim: A 3 cm tumour is T2, and 5 nodes is N2.
N1 is 1 to 3 nodes; she has 5.
N3 is 10 or more nodes, and there is no distant spread.
T3 is over 5 cm.

steps.x: C. T2 N2 M0. T2 (2–5 cm), N2 (4–9 nodes), M0.

questions.stem: A 76 year old woman has ignored a lump in her right breast for a year. There is a 4 cm hard mass with ulceration of the overlying skin and fixation to the chest wall. There are palpable axillary nodes. She feels otherwise well.
questions.q: Which is the most likely T stage?
questions.e: Any tumour involving the chest wall or skin (or inflammatory cancer) is T4, whatever its size.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely T stage? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Skin ulceration and chest wall fixation.

elim: T1 is a tumour under 2 cm.
Size alone would be T2, but skin and chest wall involvement make it T4.
T3 is over 5 cm without skin or chest wall involvement.
This is in situ disease, not an ulcerating mass.

steps.x: D. T4. Skin or chest wall involvement = T4 regardless of size.

questions.stem: A 65 year old woman had a mastectomy for breast cancer 4 years ago. She now has 3 weeks of increasing breathlessness and a dry cough. Her oxygen saturation is 93% breathing air and respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute. There is stony dullness at the right base. Chest X-ray is shown (see item resources).
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her breathlessness?
o: Malignant pleural effusion from metastatic breast cancer
questions.e: Lung and pleura are common metastatic sites of breast cancer (with bone and liver); a unilateral effusion years after treatment is a malignant effusion.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of her breathlessness? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: mastectomy for breast cancer 4 years ago
stony dullness at the right base
steps.x: Previous breast cancer and a unilateral effusion.

elim: No fever or productive cough, and stony dullness suggests fluid.
Heart failure usually causes bilateral effusions with oedema.
A pneumothorax is hyper-resonant, not stony dull.
PE does not cause a large unilateral effusion with stony dullness.

steps.x: C. Malignant pleural effusion from metastatic breast cancer. Breast cancer spreads to bone, liver and lungs.

questions.stem: A 59 year old woman treated for node-positive breast cancer 3 years ago has 2 months of fatigue, weight loss and right upper quadrant discomfort. Her liver is enlarged and craggy, 4 cm below the costal margin. She drinks 4 units of alcohol a week.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: The liver is a common site of breast cancer metastasis; craggy hepatomegaly with weight loss after breast cancer suggests liver metastases.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Cancer history, weight loss and a craggy liver.

elim: She drinks very little alcohol.
A craggy enlarged liver after cancer suggests metastases.
Gallstones do not cause a craggy hepatomegaly.
Acute viral hepatitis is not a cause of craggy hepatomegaly with weight loss.

steps.x: E. Liver metastases from breast cancer. Bone, liver and lung are the commonest metastatic sites.

questions.stem: A 42 year old woman asks about her breast cancer risk. Her menarche was at 11, she has no children, drinks 12 units of alcohol a week and her BMI is 31 kg/m2. Genetic testing after her sister's diagnosis shows she carries a pathogenic BRCA1 mutation.
questions.q: Which factor most increases her risk of breast cancer?
questions.e: All are risk factors, but heterozygous BRCA1 carriers have the highest relative risk.

steps.x: The question asks: Which factor most increases her risk of breast cancer? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Several oestrogen-related risk factors and one high-penetrance gene.

elim: Alcohol increases risk modestly.
Early menarche increases oestrogen exposure but only modestly.
Nulliparity is a modest risk factor.
Obesity is a modest risk factor, mainly after the menopause.

steps.x: B. BRCA1 mutation. BRCA1 carries the highest relative risk.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman has a painless lump in her left breast. She has taken combined HRT for 12 years, has never had children and her BMI is 33 kg/m2. Her menopause was at 56. There is a 1.8 cm hard irregular lump with skin dimpling over it.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Long HRT use, nulliparity, obesity and late menopause all increase oestrogen exposure; a hard irregular lump with skin dimpling is breast cancer.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Oestrogen-exposure risk factors and a hard lump with tethering.

elim: Cysts are smooth and mobile; a hard irregular lump with skin dimpling points to cancer.
No history of trauma.
Fibroadenomas are smooth and mobile in young women.
Lipomas are soft and do not tether the skin.

steps.x: A. Breast cancer. Hard lump + skin changes + oestrogen exposure = cancer.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man has a painless lump under his left nipple for 2 months. There is a 1.5 cm hard, irregular mass fixed to the nipple, with a palpable left axillary node. His brother had prostate cancer at 55 and his mother had breast cancer at 48. He takes no medicines.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A hard, irregular, fixed mass with axillary lymphadenopathy in a man with a family history suggests breast cancer, often linked to BRCA2.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: hard, irregular mass fixed to the nipple
steps.x: Hard, fixed, eccentric mass with a node and family history.

elim: Gynaecomastia is soft, rubbery, central and often bilateral, without a node.
Lipomas are soft and mobile.
This is fatty tissue, not a hard eccentric mass.
A smooth cyst attached to skin, not fixed to the nipple with a node.

steps.x: C. Male breast cancer. Men get breast cancer too; BRCA2 is the classic link.

questions.stem: A 57 year old woman with metastatic breast cancer has 2 weeks of headaches that are worse in the morning, with vomiting. Today her daughter says she is confused. She has a mild left-sided weakness. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 62 bpm and BP 158/90 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Raised intracranial pressure symptoms and focal signs in metastatic breast cancer indicate brain metastases, a neurological emergency.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: worse in the morning, with vomiting
steps.x: Raised ICP features with focal signs in metastatic disease.

elim: Hypercalcaemia causes confusion but not focal weakness or morning headache.
She has no fever or neck stiffness.
Migraine does not cause progressive confusion with focal weakness.
No head injury or anticoagulants; metastatic cancer is the likelier cause.

steps.x: A. Brain metastases. Neurological symptoms in breast cancer: think brain metastases.

questions.stem: A 62 year old woman with breast cancer known to have spread to bone has 1 week of worsening mid-back pain, now with weakness in both legs and difficulty passing urine. There is a sensory level at T10 and brisk reflexes in her legs.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Cauda equina syndrome from disc prolapse
questions.e: Back pain with leg weakness, a sensory level and bladder dysfunction in breast cancer with bone metastases is metastatic spinal cord compression, an emergency.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Bone metastases plus cord signs.

elim: A sensory level at T10 with brisk reflexes is a cord lesion, not cauda equina.
GBS causes areflexia, not brisk reflexes with a sensory level.
Does not usually cause a sensory level with upper motor neurone signs.
This causes distal sensory loss and reduced reflexes.

steps.x: C. Metastatic spinal cord compression. Bone mets + back pain + neuro signs = spinal cord compression.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman had a mastectomy with axillary node clearance for node-positive breast cancer 8 months ago. She now has gradual painless swelling of her right arm, which feels heavy. There is pitting oedema of the forearm and hand. She has no fever and no redness.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her arm swelling?
questions.e: Axillary node clearance removes lymphatic drainage of the arm, risking lymphoedema and functional impairment.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of her arm swelling? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: gradual painless swelling of her right arm
steps.x: Gradual, painless, one-sided arm swelling after axillary surgery.

elim: Usually sudden, painful and with venous distension.
No fever, redness or pain.
Unilateral arm swelling is not heart failure.
SVCO causes facial and bilateral arm swelling with distended neck veins.

steps.x: D. Lymphoedema after axillary node clearance. Axillary clearance risks arm lymphoedema.

questions.stem: A 45 year old woman has noticed a lump in her right breast for 3 weeks. Her GP finds a 2 cm firm, irregular lump and refers her urgently to the breast clinic. She has no family history of breast cancer.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate approach to confirm the diagnosis?
o: Clinical examination, mammography and core needle biopsy
questions.e: Triple assessment (clinical examination, imaging and core needle biopsy) is the gold standard for diagnosing breast cancer.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate approach to confirm the diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: refers her urgently to the breast clinic
steps.x: Suspicious lump in the breast clinic.

elim: CT stages disease but does not diagnose it.
Imaging alone cannot confirm cancer histologically.
MRI is not first-line and does not give tissue.
A suspicious lump needs assessment now.

steps.x: A. Clinical examination, mammography and core needle biopsy. Triple assessment is the gold standard.

questions.stem: A 63 year old woman is seen in the breast clinic with a 1.5 cm hard lump in her left breast. She has no nipple discharge. Her last screening mammogram was 2 years ago. Clinical examination has been completed.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial imaging?
questions.e: Mammography is first-line imaging over 35; ultrasound is preferred under 40 because of dense breast tissue.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial imaging? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Older woman with a lump, examination done.

elim: CT is for staging distant disease.
MRI is reserved for lobular cancer, dense breasts or high-risk screening.
PET assesses distant metastasis, not the primary lump first.
Ultrasound is first-line in younger women with dense breasts.

steps.x: B. Mammography. Over 35: mammogram; under 40: ultrasound.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman has a 1.5 cm firm, irregular lump in her right breast. She is breastfeeding her second child. Her aunt had breast cancer at 60. Clinical examination in the breast clinic has been completed.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate imaging?
questions.e: Under 40, ultrasound is the first-line imaging because breast tissue is dense.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate imaging? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Young woman with dense breast tissue.

elim: CT is not used for imaging the breast lump.
Young, dense (lactating) breasts make mammography less sensitive.
PET-CT is for distant staging.
Does not image a breast lump.

steps.x: A. Breast ultrasound. Under 40: ultrasound.

questions.stem: A 51 year old woman with no symptoms asks her GP about breast screening. She has no family history of breast or ovarian cancer and has never had a breast problem. Her friend has been told to have a mammogram every year.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate screening for her?
questions.e: The NHS Breast Screening Programme offers mammography every 3 years to women aged 50 to 70.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate screening for her? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: 51 year old woman with no symptoms
steps.x: Average-risk woman over 50.

elim: The NHS programme is 3-yearly for average-risk women.
Annual MRI is for high-risk women such as BRCA carriers.
Ultrasound is not a screening tool.
Screening starts at 50.

steps.x: C. Mammogram every 3 years until 70. NHS screening: mammogram every 3 years, ages 50–70.

questions.stem: A 56 year old woman has had spontaneous blood-stained discharge from a single duct of her right nipple for 3 weeks. There is no palpable lump and no skin change. Her left breast is normal. She takes no medicines.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Reassure: it is likely to be an intraductal papilloma
questions.e: NICE recommends 2-week-wait referral for women aged 50 or over with unilateral nipple discharge. Intraductal papilloma (benign but raises cancer risk) is a cause, but cancer must be excluded.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next step? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: blood-stained discharge from a single duct
steps.x: Over 50, unilateral, single-duct bloody discharge.

elim: There is no evidence of a prolactinoma or bilateral milky discharge.
Papilloma is a common cause but is a cancer risk and cancer must be excluded.
Over 50 with unilateral nipple discharge needs an urgent referral.
No signs of infection.

steps.x: E. Two-week-wait referral for triple assessment. Over 50 + unilateral nipple discharge = 2WW.

questions.stem: A 24 year old woman has a 1.5 cm smooth, mobile, painless lump in her left breast that she noticed 2 weeks ago. There are no skin changes, no nipple discharge and no axillary nodes. She has no family history of breast cancer.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate referral?
o: Non-urgent referral to the breast clinic
questions.e: Under NICE suspected cancer guidance, women under 30 with a lump get non-urgent referral, while those over 30 with an unexplained lump are referred urgently.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate referral? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Under 30, benign-feeling lump, no red flags.

elim: Not an emergency.
A new breast lump should be assessed.
MRI is not first-line.
Under 30 with an unexplained lump and no other features does not need an urgent cancer referral.

steps.x: C. Non-urgent referral to the breast clinic. Under 30: non-urgent; over 30: urgent referral.

questions.stem: A 60 year old woman has a 1.6 cm invasive ductal carcinoma in her left breast on core biopsy. There are no palpable axillary nodes and pre-operative axillary ultrasound is normal. She is booked for wide local excision.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate procedure to stage the axilla?
o: Fine needle aspiration of a random axillary node
questions.e: Sentinel node biopsy assesses N stage; mammography and core biopsy assess T, and PET assesses M.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate procedure to stage the axilla? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Clinically and sonographically node-negative axilla.

elim: Full clearance is for biopsy-proven nodal disease; it has higher morbidity.
CT does not reliably detect small nodal deposits.
Not a reliable staging method.
PET assesses distant metastasis (M), not small axillary nodes.

steps.x: E. Sentinel lymph node biopsy. Sentinel node biopsy stages N with less morbidity.

questions.stem: A 49 year old woman has a 2 cm invasive ductal carcinoma confirmed on core biopsy of her right breast. On examination there are no palpable axillary lymph nodes. She is being planned for surgery.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate pre-operative investigation of the axilla?
o: No assessment needed as nodes are impalpable
questions.e: Pre-operative axillary ultrasound is done when there is no palpable axillary lymphadenopathy, with biopsy of any abnormal node.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate pre-operative investigation of the axilla? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Clinically node-negative before surgery.

elim: Not used routinely.
A treatment, not a first investigation.
A bone scan looks for metastases, not axillary nodes.
Impalpable nodes can still contain cancer.

steps.x: C. Axillary ultrasound. No palpable nodes: axillary ultrasound first.

questions.stem: A 54 year old woman has a 6 cm invasive ductal carcinoma with matted axillary nodes. She has bone pain in her hip. The team needs to know whether there is distant spread before planning treatment.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to assess M stage?
o: Core needle biopsy of the breast
questions.e: Mammography and core biopsy assess T, sentinel node biopsy assesses N, and PET scan assesses M.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate investigation to assess M stage? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
The question is about metastasis staging.

elim: Assesses nodes (N), not distant spread.
Assesses the primary tumour (T) and histology.
Assesses the primary tumour.
Assesses nodes (N).

steps.x: D. PET-CT. T: mammogram/core biopsy; N: sentinel node; M: PET.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman is worried about breast cancer. Her father was diagnosed with breast cancer at 64. Her mother is well at 66 and there is no other family history of breast or ovarian cancer. She has no breast symptoms and examination is normal. She has two young children.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Annual mammography from now in primary care
No action as her mother is unaffected
Refer to a specialist familial breast cancer service
questions.e: High familial risk referral criteria include breast cancer in a first-degree male relative at any age, a first-degree relative under 40, bilateral disease under 50, or two first-degree relatives.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next step? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: father was diagnosed with breast cancer
steps.x: Male first-degree relative with breast cancer.

elim: Screening decisions follow specialist risk assessment.
No genetic risk has been established yet.
A male first-degree relative with breast cancer is high risk.
Chemoprevention needs specialist assessment first.

steps.x: D. Refer to a specialist familial breast cancer service. Male relative with breast cancer at any age: refer.

questions.stem: A 55 year old woman has a core biopsy confirming invasive lobular carcinoma of the left breast. On mammography the tumour was hard to see and its size is uncertain. The surgeon is planning breast-conserving surgery.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to define the extent of the tumour?
questions.e: Invasive lobular carcinoma is hard to detect on mammography, so MRI breast is the gold standard to assess it.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate investigation to define the extent of the tumour? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Lobular cancer poorly seen on mammogram.

elim: Does not image breast disease.
Used for distant staging.
Lobular cancer is often occult on mammography.
Stages the axilla, not the extent of the primary.

steps.x: B. MRI breast. ILC: MRI breast.

questions.stem: A 48 year old woman has a 3 cm HER2-positive invasive ductal carcinoma. The oncologist plans treatment with trastuzumab. She has no cardiac history, does not smoke and her ECG is normal. Her pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg. She has had surgery and is due to start adjuvant treatment.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation before starting trastuzumab?
questions.e: Trastuzumab carries a risk of cardiotoxicity and heart failure, so cardiac function (echocardiogram) is checked before and during treatment.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate investigation before starting trastuzumab? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
HER2 therapy and its key toxicity.

elim: Bone density monitoring is for aromatase inhibitors.
Trastuzumab is not mainly pulmonary toxic.
Hearing tests are for cisplatin.
Not the key monitoring for trastuzumab.

steps.x: B. Echocardiogram. Trastuzumab: monitor cardiac function.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman is starting letrozole after surgery for an oestrogen receptor-positive breast cancer. She went through the menopause at 51. She has no history of fractures but her mother had a hip fracture.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate baseline investigation?
questions.e: Aromatase inhibitors increase osteoporosis risk, so bone mineral density is monitored with DEXA.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate baseline investigation? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Aromatase inhibitor in a postmenopausal woman.

elim: This is for trastuzumab.
Endometrial risk is with tamoxifen, not aromatase inhibitors.
Not needed for postmenopausal women.
Not required for aromatase inhibitors.

steps.x: A. DEXA scan. AI = bone loss: check BMD with DEXA.

questions.stem: A 57 year old woman has a 1.8 cm invasive ductal carcinoma in the upper outer quadrant of her left breast. She has medium-sized breasts. Pre-operative axillary ultrasound is normal and there is no distant disease. She wants to keep her breast.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate surgical management?
o: Wide local excision with axillary node clearance
Wide local excision with sentinel lymph node biopsy
questions.e: Small (<4–5 cm) peripheral tumours with a negative axillary ultrasound are treated with breast-conserving surgery plus sentinel node biopsy.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate surgical management? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Small, peripheral, node-negative early disease.

elim: Clearance is for proven nodal spread; a small peripheral tumour suits conservation.
Surgery is the main treatment for early disease.
Radiotherapy follows surgery; it is not the primary treatment.
Her axilla is clear on ultrasound, so sentinel node biopsy is used.

steps.x: E. Wide local excision with sentinel lymph node biopsy. Early small tumour: lumpectomy + sentinel node biopsy.

questions.stem: A 62 year old woman has had a wide local excision with clear margins and a negative sentinel node biopsy for a 1.5 cm invasive ductal carcinoma. She is recovering well from surgery. The team discusses adjuvant treatment.
questions.q: Which adjuvant treatment most reduces her risk of local recurrence?
questions.e: Whole breast radiotherapy after breast-conserving surgery reduces local recurrence.

steps.x: The question asks: Which adjuvant treatment most reduces her risk of local recurrence? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: wide local excision with clear margins
steps.x: After breast-conserving surgery.

elim: Her sentinel node is negative.
Margins are clear, so further surgery is not needed.
She has early curable disease.
There is no HER2 positivity mentioned and it does not replace radiotherapy.

steps.x: E. Whole breast radiotherapy. Lumpectomy is followed by whole breast radiotherapy.

questions.stem: A 50 year old woman has a mastectomy for a 6 cm invasive ductal carcinoma. Histology shows 3 positive axillary nodes and tumour close to the deep margin. She is otherwise fit and is recovering well from surgery. CT shows no distant spread.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional treatment?
o: Wide local excision of the scar
questions.e: Adjuvant radiotherapy after mastectomy is given for T3/T4 tumours or positive nodes with residual margins.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate additional treatment? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
T3, node-positive, close margin.

elim: Not indicated without genetic risk.
T3, node-positive disease with a close margin needs radiotherapy.
Nodes are already shown to be positive.
The breast has already been removed.

steps.x: A. Adjuvant chest wall radiotherapy. Post-mastectomy radiotherapy for T3/T4 or nodal disease.

questions.stem: A 39 year old woman has a 3.5 cm invasive ductal carcinoma. Immunohistochemistry shows the tumour is oestrogen receptor-negative, progesterone receptor-negative and HER2-negative. There are positive axillary nodes. She is fit and wants the best chance of cure.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?
o: Immediate mastectomy with no systemic treatment
questions.e: Triple-negative (and node-positive) disease is treated with neoadjuvant FEC-D (fluorouracil, epirubicin, cyclophosphamide, then docetaxel), then surgery.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial treatment? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: oestrogen receptor-negative, progesterone receptor-negative and HER2-negative
steps.x: Triple-negative, node-positive.

elim: Aromatase inhibitors need ER-positive disease.
Triple-negative node-positive disease needs systemic chemotherapy.
Tamoxifen needs ER-positive disease.
Needs HER2-positive disease.

steps.x: C. Neoadjuvant FEC-D chemotherapy. Triple negative: neoadjuvant FEC-D.
